claim: Submucosal glands (SMGs) are a prominent structure that lines human cartilaginous airways.
source: Submucosal glands (SMGs) are a prominent structure that lines human cartilaginous airways.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established anatomical knowledge about human airway structure.

claim: EDA-KO pigs lacked SMGs throughout the airways.
source: EDA-KO pigs lacked SMGs throughout the airways.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in Figure 3.

claim: The airway surface liquid of EDA-KO pigs had a reduced ability to kill bacteria.
source: Their airway surface liquid had a reduced ability to kill bacteria, consistent with SMG production of antimicrobials.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: SMGs produce antimicrobials.
source: Their airway surface liquid had a reduced ability to kill bacteria, consistent with SMG production of antimicrobials.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the bacterial killing data and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: In wild-type pigs, SMGs secrete mucus that emerges onto the airway surface as strands.
source: In wild-type pigs, SMGs secrete mucus that emerges onto the airway surface as strands.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 6.

claim: Lack of SMGs and mucus strands disrupted mucociliary transport in EDA-KO pigs.
source: Lack of SMGs and mucus strands disrupted mucociliary transport in EDA-KO pigs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by ex vivo and in vivo MCT data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: EDA-KO pigs failed to eradicate a bacterial challenge in lung regions normally populated by SMGs.
source: Consequently, EDA-KO pigs failed to eradicate a bacterial challenge in lung regions normally populated by SMGs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by bacterial challenge data in Figure 8.

claim: SMGs are required for normal antimicrobial activity.
source: These in vivo and ex vivo results indicate that SMGs are required for normal antimicrobial activity and mucociliary transport, two key host defenses that protect the lung.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the bacterial killing assay data.

claim: SMGs are required for normal mucociliary transport.
source: These in vivo and ex vivo results indicate that SMGs are required for normal antimicrobial activity and mucociliary transport, two key host defenses that protect the lung.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by MCT assay data both ex vivo and in vivo.

claim: ASL serves an important protective function against infection by killing microorganisms with secreted antimicrobial peptides/proteins.
source: ASL serves an important protective function against infection by killing microorganisms with secreted antimicrobial peptides/proteins and by facilitating their removal with mucins and mucociliary transport (MCT) (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Wine and Joo, 2004; Ganz, 2002; Whitsett, 2018; Knowles and Boucher, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ASL serves an important protective function against infection by facilitating removal of microorganisms with mucins and mucociliary transport.
source: ASL serves an important protective function against infection by killing microorganisms with secreted antimicrobial peptides/proteins and by facilitating their removal with mucins and mucociliary transport (MCT) (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Wine and Joo, 2004; Ganz, 2002; Whitsett, 2018; Knowles and Boucher, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: ASL is comprised of secretions from surface epithelia lining airways and submucosal glands in the underlying submucosa.
source: ASL is comprised of secretions from two sources: surface epithelia lining airways and submucosal glands (SMGs) in the underlying submucosa.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: Both surface epithelia and SMGs produce antimicrobials and mucins.
source: Both produce antimicrobials and mucins (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Wine and Joo, 2004; Ganz, 2002; Whitsett, 2018; Knowles and Boucher, 2002; Basbaum et al., 1990; Fahy and Dickey, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Humans have abundant SMGs in their cartilaginous airways extending 8–10 airway generations to diameters of 1–2 mm.
source: Humans have abundant SMGs in their cartilaginous airways extending 8–10 airway generations to diameters of 1–2 mm (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Choi et al., 2000; Whimster, 1986).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: It has been assumed that SMGs play an important role in respiratory host defense.
source: Based on their secretory products and multiple previous studies, it has been assumed that SMGs play an important role in respiratory host defense (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Wine and Joo, 2004; Whitsett, 2018; Basbaum et al., 1990; Fahy and Dickey, 2010; Joo et al., 2015; Dajani et al., 2005; Bartlett et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The assumption that SMGs play an important role in respiratory host defense has gone without a direct in vivo test.
source: But that assumption has gone without a direct in vivo test, and it has not been possible to determine the separate contributions of SMGs and surface epithelia to airway defense.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: It has not been possible to determine the separate contributions of SMGs and surface epithelia to airway defense.
source: But that assumption has gone without a direct in vivo test, and it has not been possible to determine the separate contributions of SMGs and surface epithelia to airway defense.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Cystic fibrosis is a disease in which respiratory host defense defects cause airway infection.
source: An example is cystic fibrosis (CF), a disease in which respiratory host defense defects cause airway infection (Quinton, 1999; Stoltz et al., 2015; Quinton, 2008; Rowe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature on CF pathophysiology.

claim: CFTR is expressed in surface epithelia of proximal airways, SMG of cartilaginous airways, and surface epithelia of non-cartilaginous distal airways.
source: CFTR is expressed in surface epithelia of proximal airways, SMG of cartilaginous airways, and surface epithelia of non-cartilaginous distal airways; loss of CFTR likely impairs host defense at each of these sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about CFTR expression patterns.

claim: Loss of CFTR likely impairs host defense at surface epithelia of proximal airways, SMG of cartilaginous airways, and surface epithelia of non-cartilaginous distal airways.
source: CFTR is expressed in surface epithelia of proximal airways, SMG of cartilaginous airways, and surface epithelia of non-cartilaginous distal airways; loss of CFTR likely impairs host defense at each of these sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on CFTR expression patterns.

claim: It has been said that loss of CFTR predominantly affects distal airways and/or surface epithelia.
source: However, it has been said that loss of CFTR predominantly affects distal airways and/or surface epithelia, implying that defects in SMGs may have little role as a primary contributor to CF lung disease (Tiddens et al., 2010; Oppenheimer and Esterly, 1975; Boucher, 2019; Thelin and Boucher, 2007; Ratjen, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature expressing this view.

claim: Mice lack SMGs except in the most proximal part of the airway.
source: However, they lack SMGs except in the most proximal part of the airway, whereas humans have abundant SMGs in cartilaginous airways (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Choi et al., 2000; Meyerholz et al., 2018a; Borthwick et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: Mice have not proven to be a good model for human diseases that involve SMGs, such as cystic fibrosis.
source: Moreover, mice have not proven to be a good model for human diseases that involve SMGs, such as cystic fibrosis (CF) (Grubb and Boucher, 1999; Guilbault et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature on CF mouse models.

claim: SMGs produce multiple different antimicrobials.
source: Previous studies indicate that SMGs produce multiple different antimicrobials (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Ganz, 2002; Basbaum et al., 1990; Joo et al., 2015; Dajani et al., 2005; Bartlett et al., 2013; Fischer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides/proteins exhibit synergistic activity against bacteria.
source: A diverse complement of antimicrobial peptides/proteins may be particularly important because antimicrobials exhibit synergistic activity against bacteria (Singh et al., 2000; Abou Alaiwa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ferret trachea xenografts containing SMGs produced more antimicrobials and had greater antimicrobial activity than ferret cells seeded on denuded rat xenografts without SMGs.
source: A study of ferret trachea xenografts, which contained SMGs, transplanted into immune mice indicated that it produced more antimicrobials and had greater antimicrobial activity than ferret cells seeded on denuded rat xenografts, which did not have SMGs (Dajani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Interventions that stimulate SMG secretion increase MCT.
source: Previous studies suggest that interventions that stimulate SMG secretion increase MCT (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Wanner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Treating excised pig and ferret tracheas with acetylcholine and other agonists increased MCT.
source: For example, treating excised pig and ferret tracheas with acetylcholine and other agonists increased MCT, and inhibiting liquid secretion attenuated the increase (Ballard et al., 2002; Jeong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inhibiting liquid secretion attenuated the increase in MCT caused by acetylcholine and other agonists in excised pig and ferret tracheas.
source: For example, treating excised pig and ferret tracheas with acetylcholine and other agonists increased MCT, and inhibiting liquid secretion attenuated the increase (Ballard et al., 2002; Jeong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Pig and human lungs are similar regarding the type, amount, and distribution of airway epithelial cells and SMGs.
source: Similarity between pig and human lungs regarding the type, amount, and distribution of airway epithelial cells and SMGs; airway and lung size; airway antimicrobials; and airway transepithelial electrolyte transport make them ideal for our studies (Rogers et al., 2008; Prather et al., 2013; Judge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: Pig and human lungs are similar regarding airway and lung size.
source: Similarity between pig and human lungs regarding the type, amount, and distribution of airway epithelial cells and SMGs; airway and lung size; airway antimicrobials; and airway transepithelial electrolyte transport make them ideal for our studies (Rogers et al., 2008; Prather et al., 2013; Judge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: Pig and human lungs are similar regarding airway antimicrobials.
source: Similarity between pig and human lungs regarding the type, amount, and distribution of airway epithelial cells and SMGs; airway and lung size; airway antimicrobials; and airway transepithelial electrolyte transport make them ideal for our studies (Rogers et al., 2008; Prather et al., 2013; Judge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: Pig and human lungs are similar regarding airway transepithelial electrolyte transport.
source: Similarity between pig and human lungs regarding the type, amount, and distribution of airway epithelial cells and SMGs; airway and lung size; airway antimicrobials; and airway transepithelial electrolyte transport make them ideal for our studies (Rogers et al., 2008; Prather et al., 2013; Judge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior comparative studies.

claim: SMGs are present at birth in pigs.
source: In addition, because SMGs are present at birth, pigs can be studied as newborns, thereby avoiding secondary consequences of disease.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for studying newborn pigs.

claim: Genetically modified pigs provide a good model for airway disease such as CF.
source: Genetically modified pigs also provide a good model for airway disease such as CF, where they have highlighted the importance of antimicrobial peptides/proteins and MCT for host defense (Hoegger et al., 2014; Stoltz et al., 2010; Pezzulo et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2016; Ermund et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies using pig models of CF.

claim: Formation of glands and other epithelial appendages like hair and teeth is initiated by the ectodysplasin pathway.
source: Formation of glands and other epithelial appendages like hair and teeth is initiated by the ectodysplasin pathway (Rawlins and Hogan, 2005; Laurikkala et al., 2002; Mikkola, 2009; Jaskoll et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature on developmental biology.

claim: The ectodysplasin pathway includes the soluble ligand ectodysplasin A (EDA), the EDA receptor EDAR, and the EDA transducer EDARADD.
source: This pathway includes the soluble ligand ectodysplasin A (EDA), the EDA receptor EDAR, and the EDA transducer EDARADD.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about the ectodysplasin pathway.

claim: Mutations in each of the genes in the ectodysplasin pathway have been reported in humans who develop hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED).
source: Mutations in each of the genes in this pathway have been reported in humans who develop the disease hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED) (Pääkkönen et al., 2001; Kere et al., 1996; Cluzeau et al., 2011; Schneider et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior clinical and genetic studies.

claim: HED defects include loss or reduction in glands, hair, and teeth.
source: HED defects include loss or reduction in glands, hair, and teeth (Dietz et al., 2013; Clarke et al., 1987; Capitanio et al., 1968; Reed et al., 1970).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: There are variable reports of recurrent respiratory tract infections, asthma-like symptoms, and otitis media in HED patients.
source: There are also variable reports of recurrent respiratory tract infections, asthma-like symptoms, and otitis media (Dietz et al., 2013; Clarke et al., 1987; Reed et al., 1970; Callea et al., 2013; Beahrs et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: EDA mutations in mice, dogs, and cattle cause loss of nasal, submandibular, and submucosal glands.
source: EDA mutations in mice, dogs, and cattle cause loss of nasal, submandibular, and submucosal glands, and there are limited reports investigating respiratory symptoms and mucus accumulation (Jaskoll et al., 2003; Azar et al., 2016; Casal et al., 2005a; Seeliger et al., 2005; Vasiliadis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: Exon 4 of the EDA gene encodes the collagen domain.
source: To generate pigs lacking SMG, we targeted exon 4 of the EDA gene; exon 4 encodes the collagen domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing was used to generate EDA-KO pigs.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing, injecting the guide RNAs and Cas9 mRNA into porcine zygotes (Yuan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Redel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior methods papers.

claim: Four litters of EDA-KO pigs were generated.
source: We generated four litters, and in all the piglets, we found indels in exon 4 that predicted a loss of function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of the experimental outcome.

claim: All piglets in the four EDA-KO litters had indels in exon 4 that predicted a loss of function.
source: We generated four litters, and in all the piglets, we found indels in exon 4 that predicted a loss of function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: EDA-KO pigs had birth weights similar to those of wild-type controls.
source: EDA-KO pigs had birth weights (1.48 ± 0.48 kg, mean ± SD, n = 20) similar to those of wild-type controls (1.54 ± 0.31 kg, n = 18) (p=0.94).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific numerical data and statistical analysis.

claim: The EDA gene is located on the X chromosome.
source: Of note, the EDA gene is located on the X chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established genetic knowledge.

claim: No sex differences were observed in EDA-KO piglets on initial exam.
source: However, on initial exam, we could discern no sex differences in EDA-KO piglets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the study.

claim: EDA-KO piglets began sneezing within hours of birth and sneezing persisted.
source: The only observed difference in behavior of EDA-KO piglets was sneezing; sneezing began within hours of birth and persisted.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the study.

claim: EDA-KO pigs had sparse hair on the back distributed as linear patterns of hairy stripes alternating with hairless skin.
source: EDA-KO pigs had sparse hair on the back distributed as linear patterns of hairy stripes alternating with hairless skin (Figure 2B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EDA-KO pigs had a bald circular patch on the top of their heads.
source: They had a bald circular patch on the top of their heads (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EDA-KO piglets lacked hair on their upper and lower eyelids but retained eyelashes.
source: EDA-KO piglets also lacked hair on their upper and lower eyelids but retained eyelashes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The body hair phenotypes of EDA-KO pigs are similar to those reported for other animals with mutations in the ectodysplasin pathway.
source: These body hair phenotypes are similar to those reported for other animals with mutations in the ectodysplasin pathway (Vasiliadis et al., 2019; Casal et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior animal studies.

claim: The conducting airways of wild-type pigs had SMGs.
source: The conducting airways of wild-type pigs had SMGs (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: In wild-type pigs, the numbers of SMGs decreased from proximal trachea to bronchi and bronchioles.
source: As is observed in humans (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Choi et al., 2000; Whimster, 1986; Meyerholz et al., 2018a), the numbers of SMGs decreased from proximal trachea to bronchi and bronchioles.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior anatomical studies and data in Figure 3B.

claim: Airways of EDA-KO piglets lacked SMGs.
source: In contrast, airways of EDA-KO piglets lacked SMGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: EDA-KO pigs lacked glands in other tissues.
source: Consistent with loss of airway SMGs, EDA-KO pigs lacked glands in other tissues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B are expressed in airway surface epithelia of humans and pigs.
source: Mucins MUC5AC and MUC5B are expressed in airway surface epithelia of humans and pigs (Fahy and Dickey, 2010; Ostedgaard et al., 2017; Ermund et al., 2017; Okuda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Immunostaining revealed no difference in the localization of MUC5AC or MUC5B in surface epithelia of EDA-KO and wild-type airways.
source: Immunostaining revealed no difference in the localization of MUC5AC or MUC5B in surface epithelia of EDA-KO and wild-type airways (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ciliated marker β-tubulin IV showed similar immunostaining patterns in EDA-KO and wild-type piglets.
source: The ciliated marker β-tubulin IV also showed similar immunostaining patterns in EDA-KO and wild-type piglets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SMG cells produce lysozyme and lactoferrin.
source: It is well known that SMG cells produce a variety of antimicrobials, including lysozyme and lactoferrin (Basbaum et al., 1990; Joo et al., 2015; Dajani et al., 2005; Fischer et al., 2009; Widdicombe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: By 1 min, ASL in wild-type piglets killed approximately half of the bacteria.
source: By 1 min, ASL in wild-type piglets killed approximately half of the bacteria (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ASL in EDA-KO piglets killed less than one-quarter of the bacteria by 1 min.
source: In contrast, ASL in EDA-KO piglets killed less than one-quarter of the bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Loss of SMGs impairs antimicrobial activity on the proximal airway surface.
source: These results indicate that loss of SMGs impairs antimicrobial activity on the proximal airway surface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the bacterial killing data.

claim: Acinar cells in SMGs of pigs and humans produce MUC5B.
source: Acinar cells in SMGs of pigs and humans produce MUC5B, a secreted gel-forming mucin that is the major structural protein of SMG mucus (Ostedgaard et al., 2017; Ermund et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2007; Thornton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: MUC5B is the major structural protein of SMG mucus.
source: Acinar cells in SMGs of pigs and humans produce MUC5B, a secreted gel-forming mucin that is the major structural protein of SMG mucus (Ostedgaard et al., 2017; Ermund et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2007; Thornton et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In pigs and humans, mucus emerges from SMG ducts onto the airway surface in the form of strands.
source: In pigs and humans, mucus emerges from SMG ducts onto the airway surface in the form of strands (Hoegger et al., 2014; Ermund et al., 2018; Ostedgaard et al., 2017; Ermund et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2019; Tipirneni et al., 2018; Trillo-Muyo et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mucus strands sweep across the airway surface propelled by cilia and bind particulate material and bacteria.
source: Mucus strands sweep across the airway surface propelled by cilia and bind particulate material and bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about mucus strand function.

claim: During a 15-min observation period, hundreds of mucus strands crossed the field in wild-type piglet airways.
source: During a 15-min observation period, hundreds of mucus strands crossed the field in wild-type piglet airways (Figure 6A and B, Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B and Video 1.

claim: EDA-KO airways had no or trivial numbers of mucus strands.
source: In contrast, EDA-KO airways had no or trivial numbers of mucus strands (Figure 6A and B, Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B and Video 2.

claim: Ciliary beating was similar in wild-type and EDA-KO piglets.
source: Ciliary beating was similar in wild-type and EDA-KO piglets, indicating that the lack of mucus strands was not due to reduced ciliary activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lack of mucus strands in EDA-KO airways was not due to reduced ciliary activity.
source: Ciliary beating was similar in wild-type and EDA-KO piglets, indicating that the lack of mucus strands was not due to reduced ciliary activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the ciliary beat frequency data.

claim: In wild-type airways, mucus strands sweeping over the surface often wrapped around metallic spheres and pulled them off to the edge of the tracheal segment.
source: In wild-type airways, mucus strands sweeping over the surface often wrapped around the spheres and pulled them off to the edge of the tracheal segment, as we previously reported (Figure 6D and E, Video 3; Fischer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D and E and Video 3.

claim: Without mucus strands in EDA-KO airways, metallic spheres less frequently moved.
source: However, without mucus strands in EDA-KO airways to initiate movement, spheres less frequently moved (Figure 6D and E, Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E and Video 4.

claim: In EDA-KO airways, bits of mucus attached to the spheres, but instead of clearing spheres to the edge of the airway segment, the spheres spun in place due to the action of the underlying cilia.
source: Bits of mucus attached to the spheres, but instead of clearing spheres to the edge of the airway segment, the spheres spun in place due to the action of the underlying cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Video 4.

claim: Under basal conditions, individual microdisks followed a trajectory toward the larynx in wild-type piglets.
source: Under basal conditions, individual microdisks followed a trajectory toward the larynx in wild-type piglets, consistent with earlier results (Figure 7A, Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Video 5.

claim: Under basal conditions, microdisks showed little movement in EDA-KO piglets.
source: In contrast, microdisks showed little movement in EDA-KO piglets (Figure 7A, Video 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Video 6.

claim: Under basal conditions, the percentage of time that microdisks were in motion was decreased in EDA-KO pigs compared to wild-type.
source: This difference was reflected in a decreased percentage of time that microdisks were in motion in EDA-KO pigs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Under basal conditions, the speed of disks that did move was similar in both wild-type and EDA-KO piglets.
source: The speed of disks that did move was similar in both wild-type and EDA-KO piglets (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Under basal conditions, there was a non-statistically significant trend toward decreased clearance of microdisks from the lungs of EDA-KO piglets.
source: These changes were associated with a non-statistically significant trend toward decreased clearance of microdisks from the lungs of EDA-KO piglets under basal conditions (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: After methacholine stimulation, microdisks in wild-type piglets followed a trajectory up the large airways and were in motion for most of the time.
source: In wild-type piglets, microdisks followed a trajectory up the large airways and were in motion for most of the time (Figure 7A and B, Video 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and B and Video 7.

claim: After methacholine stimulation, there was less movement of microdisks in EDA-KO piglets compared to wild-type.
source: There was less movement in EDA-KO piglets (Figure 7A and B, Video 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and B and Video 8.

claim: After methacholine stimulation, for microdisks that did move, there was a non-statistically significant trend for a decreased mean speed in EDA-KO piglets.
source: For microdisks that did move, there was a non-statistically significant trend for a decreased mean speed in EDA-KO piglets (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: After methacholine stimulation, EDA-KO piglets failed to clear microdisks from the lung during the course of the study, in contrast to wild-type piglets.
source: In contrast to wild-type piglets, EDA-KO piglets failed to clear microdisks from the lung during the course of the study (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Loss of SMGs in EDA-KO piglets impaired MCT in vivo.
source: These findings indicate that loss of SMGs in EDA-KO piglets impaired MCT in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the in vivo MCT data.

claim: EDA-KO piglets had ~10,000 times more S. aureus in tracheal washes than wild-type piglets 4 hours after aerosolization.
source: EDA-KO piglets had ~10,000 times more S. aureus in tracheal washes than wild-type piglets (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: EDA-KO piglets had ~100 times more S. aureus in BAL liquid than wild-type piglets 4 hours after aerosolization.
source: EDA-KO piglets had ~100 times more S. aureus in BAL liquid than wild-type piglets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Counts of S. aureus in lung homogenates did not statistically differ between EDA-KO and wild-type piglets 4 hours after aerosolization.
source: Counts of S. aureus did not statistically differ between EDA-KO and wild-type piglets, although there was a trend for fewer sterile airways in EDA-KO piglets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8.

claim: There was a trend for fewer sterile airways in EDA-KO piglets compared to wild-type in lung homogenates.
source: Counts of S. aureus did not statistically differ between EDA-KO and wild-type piglets, although there was a trend for fewer sterile airways in EDA-KO piglets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation from the data in Figure 8.

claim: EDA-KO pigs may be less able to eliminate viable bacteria in large airways where SMGs are located than in more distal lung regions that lack SMGs.
source: Although the quantitative delivery to and relative recovery of S. aureus in various airway regions is unknown, the data suggest that EDA-KO pigs may be less able to eliminate viable bacteria in large airways where SMGs are located than in more distal lung regions that lack SMGs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the bacterial challenge data.

claim: Distal airway host defenses might be relatively spared in EDA-KO pigs.
source: We speculate that distal airway host defenses might be relatively spared in EDA-KO pigs, although similar studies done at varying times after bacteria delivery could be revealing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation based on the bacterial challenge data.

claim: Airway SMGs protect the lung by contributing to bacterial killing by ASL.
source: These results indicate that airway SMGs protect the lung by contributing to two critical respiratory host defenses, bacterial killing by ASL and production of strands of mucus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Airway SMGs protect the lung by contributing to production of strands of mucus.
source: These results indicate that airway SMGs protect the lung by contributing to two critical respiratory host defenses, bacterial killing by ASL and production of strands of mucus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: When challenged with S. aureus, EDA-KO lungs were compromised in their ability to eradicate bacteria, especially in regions normally populated by SMGs.

claim: The study provides direct evidence that SMGs play a critical role in host defense, both in vivo and ex vivo.
source: Our findings provide direct evidence for that hypothesis, both in vivo and ex vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: One potential advantage of having SMGs is that they markedly expand the number of epithelial cells available to produce antimicrobials and mucus and deliver them onto the airway surface.
source: One potential advantage is that SMGs markedly expand the number of epithelial cells available to produce antimicrobials and mucus and deliver them onto the airway surface (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Choi et al., 2000; Reid, 1960).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Innervation of SMGs by vagal cholinergic efferents enables them to rapidly secrete SMG products on demand.
source: In addition, innervation of SMGs by vagal cholinergic efferents enables them to rapidly secrete SMG products on demand (Wine, 2007; Widdicombe, 2002; Ballard and Spadafora, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ability to quickly deliver copious amounts of antimicrobials, mucins, and other mucus products could be critically important for responding to acute challenges such as aspiration, irritants, and pathogens.
source: The ability to quickly deliver copious amounts of antimicrobials, mucins, and other mucus products could be critically important for responding to acute challenges such as aspiration, irritants, and pathogens.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation about the functional significance of SMGs.

claim: Strands of mucus bind to large particles and transmit forces from beating cilia, thereby initiating and sustaining particle transport up the airways and out of the lung.
source: Our ex vivo and in vivo data and earlier reports indicate that strands of mucus bind to large particles and transmit forces from beating cilia, thereby initiating and sustaining particle transport up the airways and out of the lung (Hoegger et al., 2014; Fischer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the study's data and citations to prior work.

claim: Disrupting mucus strands by breaking disulfide cross links between mucin molecules impairs MCT.
source: Consistent with these findings, disrupting mucus strands by breaking disulfide cross links between mucin molecules impairs MCT (Fischer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In addition to the abundance of mucus that SMGs produce, the unique architecture of mucus strands may be important for host defense in cartilaginous airways.
source: Thus, in addition to the abundance of mucus that SMGs produce, the unique architecture of mucus strands may be important for host defense in cartilaginous airways.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: In pigs and humans, SMGs line the large cartilaginous airways, decrease in number as the airways become smaller, and are absent in very small airways.
source: In pigs and humans, SMGs line the large cartilaginous airways, decrease in number as the airways become smaller, and are absent in very small airways.

claim: SMGs are present where the velocity and turbulence of air flow deposit most large particulate material, and they are missing in the small distal airways that large particles do not reach.
source: Thus, SMGs are present where the velocity and turbulence of air flow deposit most large particulate material, and they are missing in the small distal airways that large particles do not reach.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the anatomical distribution of SMGs.

claim: Locating SMGs in larger airways positions the mucus strands they produce at sites where they can facilitate removal of impacted large particles.
source: Locating SMGs in larger airways positions the mucus strands they produce at sites where they can facilitate removal of impacted large particles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the functional significance of SMG distribution.

claim: There is a positive relationship between tracheal diameter and SMG volume across species.
source: This relationship between airway size and the presence of SMGs holds across a variety of species, with a positive relationship between tracheal diameter and SMG volume (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015; Choi et al., 2000).

claim: In small mammals such as mice and rabbits, the lung's airways have few or no SMGs.

claim: In the trachea of horses, the number of SMGs is similar to that of man and other large mammals, but the volume of individual glands is smaller.
source: Interestingly, in the trachea of a large mammal, the horse, the number of SMGs is similar to that of man and other large mammals, but the volume of individual glands is smaller (Widdicombe and Pecson, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Horses are obligate nose breathers.
source: Horses are obligate nose breathers, and their long, complex nasal turbinates may prevent most large particles from reaching the lung (Widdicombe and Wine, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The long, complex nasal turbinates of horses may prevent most large particles from reaching the lung.
